title: Talk, Judge, Cooperate: Gossip-Driven Indirect Reciprocity in Self-Interested LLM Agents
one_liner: ALIGN uses decentralized gossip to build reputations so self-interested agents cooperate with helpful peers and isolate defectors.
lead: Indirect reciprocity means an agent helps someone because that someone helped others earlier. This pattern is hard to sustain when agents are decentralized and self-interested, because each agent sees only a small slice of the past and cannot rely on a central reputation server. ALIGN addresses this by letting agents exchange structured gossip that carries reputational judgments, helping the group identify defectors and keep cooperation alive.

paras: A self-interested agent has no built-in reason to help another agent today if that help has a cost, because helping uses time or resources right away. Cooperation survives only if helping now improves future treatment from the group, because later partners reward a good reputation.

That is hard in decentralized settings because no single agent sees the full history. A defector can exploit this gap by taking help from others and refusing to return it. If agents cannot spread reliable reputational information, then helpful agents get little reward and cooperation fades.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Let agents spread structured gossip about past behavior so each agent can update reputations locally and choose partners based on those reputations.

panels.title: 1. Agents meet with limited history
panels.viz_args: Agent A knows what B did to A, but not what B did to C or D.
panels.caption: Local interaction history is too narrow to support group-wide trust.

panels.title: 2. Defectors exploit the blind spots
panels.caption: A selfish agent can look acceptable to one peer while harming others.

panels.title: 3. Gossip spreads behavior reports
panels.viz_args: A tells C that B refused to help after receiving help.
panels.caption: Agents share observations so reputations can travel beyond direct interaction.

panels.title: 4. Local reputations update
panels.viz_args: C lowers B's reputation and avoids B in the next round.
panels.caption: Each agent keeps its own trust record instead of depending on a central authority.

panels.title: 5. Cooperation becomes stable again
panels.caption: Helpful agents find each other more often because defectors are identified and excluded.

steps.text: Each round produces local evidence about who helped, who refused, and under what conditions.
They share open-ended reports about recent interactions so reputational information can travel through the network.

steps.b: Each agent updates local trust scores
steps.text: Incoming gossip changes how much an agent trusts others, especially when it matches direct experience.

steps.b: Future partner choices depend on trust
steps.text: Agents are more willing to help peers with good reputations because that increases the chance of future reciprocal treatment.
Once bad reports spread, fewer agents cooperate with the defector, which lowers the payoff of selfish behavior.

paras: The paper changes how reputational information moves through the agent society. Instead of relying only on direct experience, it lets agents exchange linguistic reports that shape later cooperation choices.

hidden.name: Local trust estimate
paras: A local trust estimate is each agent's private belief about whether another agent is worth helping. It is hidden because there is no central reputation board. Each agent has only a personal score built from direct interactions and gossip it has heard.

ALIGN improves the quality of these local estimates because gossip carries information that would otherwise stay trapped in separate pairwise encounters. That broader information makes it harder for a defector to look good to everyone at once, because reports from several peers expose a repeated pattern of selfish behavior.

heat.caption: Darker means an agent is more likely to be treated as untrustworthy.

reads.html: This is each agent's current answer to the question, should I cooperate with this other agent?
The trust estimate is updated from direct outcomes and from gossip reports, which lets indirect reciprocity emerge without a central reputation system.

paras: Gossip helps because it widens the information horizon of each agent. A defector survives when bad behavior stays local. Once reports spread, the defector's future partners can respond before being exploited themselves, so selfish behavior becomes less profitable.

The method also helps preserve cooperation because good behavior becomes visible beyond one pairwise encounter. An agent that helps others builds a better reputation across the group, which leads to more future cooperation opportunities and higher long-run payoff because more partners are willing to choose that agent again.

stages.s: Share gossip reports across the network

math.words: Each agent updates another agent's trust score by combining direct interaction evidence with weighted gossip from peers.
math.equation: trust_(t+1)(j) = trust_t(j) + direct_t(j) + sum_k w_k * gossip_k(j)
symbols: the current trust score for agent j before the update
the effect of the latest direct interaction with agent j
peer k's report about agent j
how much weight to give peer k's report
the updated trust score for agent j

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Agent C has neutral trust in agent B.
C hears from A that B accepted help but refused to return help later.
C also sees B ignore a small request directly.
The direct term is negative because C observed refusal.
The gossip term is also negative because A reported the same pattern.
B's trust score drops, so C declines to help B in the next round.

math.note: The exact policy in the paper is richer than this toy rule, but the idea is the same: trust moves up or down from direct evidence and shared reports.

charts.title: No gossip baseline
charts.note: Without gossip, bad behavior stays hidden longer, so defectors keep finding partners.

charts.title: ALIGN
charts.note: The paper reports stronger cooperation because gossip makes partner selection respond to broader social history.

items.html: If agents spread inaccurate reports, then good agents may be punished unfairly because later partner choices are based on bad information.
If one bad report causes a large reputation drop, then the society can become too unforgiving because small mistakes are treated like persistent defection.
A malicious new agent may keep re-entering with no history, which weakens reputation tracking unless the society has ways to treat unknown entrants cautiously.
The method works best when gossip is informative enough to separate real defectors from helpful peers, because then partner choice aligns long-run payoff with cooperative behavior.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Simulate a small society of ten agents that repeatedly decide whether to help each other at a cost, because cooperation must trade an immediate sacrifice for later social return. Compare two settings: direct experience only, and direct experience plus gossip-based reputation updates. Track cooperation rate, average payoff, and how quickly defectors become isolated. The demo should show that gossip sustains indirect reciprocity because it spreads reputational evidence beyond one-to-one encounters.
demo.metric_eq: cooperation_rate = helping_actions / interaction_rounds ; welfare = total_group_payoff / interaction_rounds
demo.closing: The demo must show that defectors lose partners faster when gossip is available, because bad reports travel beyond their direct victims.
